The Family Court House (Familieretshuset). If they still cannot agree, the Family Court House or the courts can decide on contact, custody and residence.
Who visits newborn children at home, and does it cost anything?
A health visitor (sundhedsplejerske). The visits are free.
Until when can a woman have an abortion?
Before the end of the 18th week of pregnancy. It is free, and the woman decides for herself.
What permission does an abortion require if the woman is under 18?
Permission from her parents (in special cases she can apply without it).
What can you get if you are not paid during maternity/parental leave?
Parental leave benefit (barselsdagpenge) (you must have earned the right through work or an a-kasse).
May you hit children in Denmark?
No – it is forbidden.
From what age may children normally have paid work outside the home?
13 (children under 13 normally may not).
What is the age of sexual consent?
15 – it is forbidden to have sex with young people under 15.
From what age can you be punished?
From 15. Children under 15 cannot be punished.
How old must you be to buy ordinary beer?
16 years.
How old must you be to buy very strong beer, wine, spirits and cigarettes?
How old must you be to get a driving licence for a car?
17 years.
What rules apply to 17-year-olds with a driving licence?
They may drive without a companion from 5:00 to 20:00. From 20:00 to 5:00 they must have a companion over 24 who has held a licence for at least five years.
When do you come of age in Denmark, and what does it mean?
At 18. You have the right to vote, can borrow money from the bank and are responsible for yourself.
What is your duty if you know about violence or abuse against children under 18?
To contact the municipality and report it.
Do the authorities have to approve an association before it is formed?
No. Everyone (including foreigners) has the right to form an association.
Which three freedoms is the right to form associations linked to?
Freedom of association, freedom of assembly and freedom of speech (in the Constitution).
What does it mean to be a volunteer?
To do work for the association without being paid.
Where does associations' money come from?
Members' fees, public grants and private actors (foundations and companies).
What is a homework café (lektiecafé)?
Volunteers help schoolchildren with their homework.
What is a friendship family (venskabsfamilie)?
One family helps another family that needs support (e.g. with the children's schooling or childcare).
What is a mentoring scheme?
A mentor gives advice and guidance to, for example, a student who needs support.
What is a drop-in centre (værested)?
A place where, for example, homeless people can get a meal or a cup of coffee.
What is a visiting friend (besøgsven)?
A volunteer who visits lonely elderly people.
What are BørneTelefonen and Livslinjen?
BørneTelefonen: telephone counselling for children and young people with problems. Livslinjen: counselling for people with suicidal thoughts.
Are there exams at evening schools (aftenskoler)?
No. You have to pay to attend.
Name adult education associations that run evening schools.
AOF, LOF, FOF, DOF and FORA.
How many folk high schools (højskoler) are there in Denmark?
About 70.
How long are short and long courses at folk high schools?
Short: about a week (often in the summer holidays). Long: usually three to five months.
Who was Grundtvig, and what does he mean for the folk high schools?
Nikolaj Frederik Severin Grundtvig (1783–1872), poet and priest. His ideas inspired the folk high schools – education for everyone creates democracy.
Are there exams at folk high schools?
No. You learn for your own sake, not for grades.
What do you need to borrow from the library?
A health insurance card or a library card.
What are eReolen and Filmstriben?
The libraries' free online services for borrowing/streaming e-books and audiobooks (eReolen) and films and TV series (Filmstriben).
When do you get the health insurance card?
When you are registered in the CPR (the Central Person Register) in a municipality.
What does it cost to see your GP?
What does it mean that the doctor 'refers' a patient?
The doctor sends the patient to a specialist, physiotherapist or hospital. You do not need a referral for an emergency hospital visit.
What is the difference between prescription medicine and over-the-counter medicine?
Prescription medicine requires a prescription from the doctor (only at a pharmacy). Over-the-counter medicine can be bought without a prescription – also in some supermarkets.
Who runs the public hospitals?
The Danish regions. Treatment is free.
What does outpatient treatment (ambulant behandling) mean?
Examination or treatment without being admitted.
What must you do before turning up at the emergency department?
Call the emergency department first.
What is free choice of hospital?
That you can normally choose yourself which public hospital you want to be treated at.
When can you be referred to a private hospital free of charge?
If you would have to wait more than a month for treatment at a public hospital.
Are you entitled to an interpreter at the doctor's or at the hospital?
Yes. In some cases you have to pay a fee.
Up to what age is dental care free for children and young people?
Up to and including 21 (in the municipality where you live).
What do adults pay for the dentist?
Adults from 22 choose a private dentist themselves and pay themselves – with a public subsidy.
How many preventive child health check-ups can a child get, and when?
Seven check-ups at the doctor's, from when the child is five weeks old until five years.
Are childhood vaccinations free?
Yes – given by the GP. You pay for travel vaccinations yourself.
What are lifestyle diseases?
Diseases linked to the way you live, e.g. smoking, alcohol or fatty food.
What is the age limit for buying alcohol over six percent?
18 (beer under 6% from 16). In nightlife zones: 18 to buy alcohol after 22:00.
Where is it forbidden to smoke indoors?
In public places (buses, sports halls, cinemas), workplaces, schools and the vast majority of restaurants, cafés, bars and nightclubs.
Where must tobacco products and e-cigarettes be placed in shops?
Hidden away so that customers cannot see them.
What do equal treatment and equality mean?
That all citizens must be treated equally regardless of gender, ethnic origin or religion.
On which grounds may you not discriminate in working life?
Gender, race, skin colour, religion or belief, political opinion, sexual orientation, age, disability, national/social/ethnic background.
What does the law say about equal pay?
Men and women are entitled to the same pay for the same work.
Where can you complain about illegal discrimination, and does it cost anything?
The Board of Equal Treatment (Ligebehandlingsnævnet). It is free to complain.
In 1915 (through a constitutional amendment).
When was Denmark's first free constitution signed?
How many of the Folketing's 179 members are women?
86 (48 percent).
Who was Denmark's first female minister?
Nina Bang – Minister of Education in 1924.
Helle Thorning-Schmidt in 2011.
What obligations do spouses have towards each other?
Both have a duty to support each other and their children.
Do women and men have the right to a divorce even if their spouse does not want it?
Who decides over a person's wages and money?
The person themselves (everyone over 18) – whether married, woman or man.
What is the rainbow flag a symbol of?
LGBT+ people.
What is Denmark's constitution called?
The Constitutional Act of the Kingdom of Denmark (Grundloven).
When did Denmark get its first Constitution, and when was it last amended?
First: 1849. Most recent amendment: 1953.
What is required to amend the Constitution?
The sitting Folketing passes the proposal → new election → the new Folketing passes it unchanged → referendum. Requires a majority of those voting and at least 40% of all voters.
What was the age for voting and for being elected to the Folketing in 1849?
You had to be 30 to vote and 25 to be elected (men only). Today it is 18.
What is freedom of speech, and what is its limit?
The right to say and write publicly what you think, without prior approval. Statements must not be illegal (e.g. defamation and racism) – otherwise you can be punished afterwards.
What is freedom of assembly, and when must the police be told?
The right to gather for public meetings and demonstrations. The police must be notified at least 24 hours in advance (otherwise you can be fined).
What is freedom of association, and what is its limit?
The right to form associations with a lawful purpose without permission. Associations with a violent purpose can be dissolved – the courts decide.
What does the inviolability of the home mean?
That, as a rule, the police may not enter people's homes without a judge's approval.
What does personal liberty mean in relation to arrest?
An arrested person must be brought before a judge within 24 hours.
What does the Constitution say about religion?
You can choose your own religion (freedom of religion). The Danish national church (folkekirken) has a special status and is supported by the state.
What is a monarchy?
A form of government with a monarch (king or queen) as head of state.
Who is Denmark's king, and when did he inherit the throne?
King Frederik X – in 2024, after his mother, Queen Margrethe II.
Who inherits the throne after Frederik X?
Crown Prince Christian (the monarch's eldest child inherits the throne).
What political power does the king have?
None. He signs laws together with a minister and has official functions when a government is formed.
Who is married to King Frederik X, and where is she from?
Queen Mary, from Australia (married since 2004). They have four children.
What are the names of Frederik X's children?
Crown Prince Christian, Princess Isabella and the twins Prince Vincent and Princess Josephine.
When does the king give his New Year's speech?
Every year on New Year's Eve, 31 December (shown on TV).
What was absolute monarchy (enevælde), and how long did it last?
A form of government where the king held power alone – from 1660–61 to 1849.
Who was Denmark's last absolute monarch?
Frederik VII (became king in 1848 and gave up power).
What is the separation of powers?
Legislative power (government + Folketing), executive power (the government) and judicial power (the courts).
The government and the Folketing together.
Who holds the executive power?
The government (ministers and civil servants make sure the laws are carried out).
The courts – they are independent.
What is the purpose of the separation of powers?
That the Folketing can control the government, and that the courts can assess whether decisions and laws are lawful and compatible with the Constitution.
Who signs a bill that has been passed?
The King and a minister – then the law is published.
What is the job of the police?
To maintain peace and order and to prevent, investigate and solve crime.
May the police use violence or threats during questioning?
How long may the police hold an arrested person before the person must go before a judge?
At most 24 hours – otherwise the person must be released.
Who decides whether a person should be punished?
The courts (the police investigate).
What does it mean that the courts are independent?
The government and the Folketing cannot decide how they rule and cannot dismiss a judge. Judges follow only the laws.
How many district courts are there, and what can you do after a district court ruling?
24 district courts (plus the Maritime and Commercial Court). You can normally appeal to the High Court.
What are the two High Courts called, and where are they?
The Eastern High Court (Østre Landsret) in Copenhagen and the Western High Court (Vestre Landsret) in Viborg.
What is Denmark's highest court called?
The Supreme Court (Højesteret).
What are the usual punishments in Denmark, and what is the harshest?
A fine or prison. Harshest: life imprisonment. There is no death penalty.
What is the difference between a suspended and an unconditional prison sentence?
An unconditional sentence must be served. A suspended one can be avoided if you meet conditions (e.g. no new crime, community service).
What is a criminal record certificate, and how long does information stay on the private one?
A document that shows whether you have been convicted. Information on the private certificate is removed after two to five years.
What happens if a child under 15 does something criminal?
Children under 15 cannot be punished. The authorities can, however, place the child outside the home or impose activities.
What is Denmark's parliament called, and where does it work?
The Folketing – at Christiansborg in Copenhagen.
179: 175 elected in Denmark, two in the Faroe Islands and two in Greenland.
Which power does the Folketing make up together with the government?
The legislative power.
The Folketing.
What are the Folketing's most important tasks besides legislation?
